system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. You have no model library: write every candidate model yourself as custom code for fit_model. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms.
3. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
4. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
5. Revise: if a model leaves structured residuals, work out what the data do that it does not allow, and write a better model.
6. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
7. Submit with submit_model (mechanism_label 'custom'), citing fit_ids as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 20 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates at substrate levels outside the measured range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Inspect data: S range, v pattern, replicate structure
Fit Michaelis-Menten (mm) and substrate inhibition models with additive error
Compare BIC and residuals; check for structure at high S

content.thinking: The low-S data look sigmoidal: flat near zero, a steep rise between 2 and 4, then saturation. A Hill-type model with cooperativity could capture that, and I'm considering whether a lag or threshold term is needed too. I'll fit the Hill form first, then check whether an offset improves it.

content.text: The Michaelis-Menten fit leaves clear structured residuals, and the data look sigmoidal at low S (near zero up to 1.5, then a steep rise). The substrate-inhibition fit ran to a degenerate solution. I'll try a Hill (cooperative) model next.

content.thinking: I'm checking the Hill fit: BIC is -39.6 with no leftover structure in the residuals, and n comes out to 2.8. The data at 16 sit near 9.9 with no drop-off, so I don't see a case for a substrate-inhibition tail. I'm settling on the Hill model, with moderate-to-high confidence.

content.text: The Hill model removes the structure in the residuals, so I'll record it and submit.

input.evidence: fit3: Vmax 9.92 (2%), K 3.08 (3%), n 2.78 (6%); BIC -39.6 vs 10.1 for MM (fit1); no residual trend vs S (rho 0.03), runs z=0.46

input.summary: The rate is sigmoidal in S: near zero up to ~1.5 uM, then a steep rise and saturation near 10 uM/min. Michaelis-Menten (fit1, BIC 10.1) leaves strong structured residuals, and a substrate-inhibition model (fit2) degenerates with no real improvement, since the rate does not fall at high S. A Hill model (fit3) with Vmax 9.92, K 3.08 and n 2.78 (about 2-6% relative SE) fits with no residual structure (BIC -39.6). The Hill coefficient near 3 suggests cooperative substrate binding; the data cannot distinguish this from other sigmoidal mechanisms without inhibitor or more points in the 1-4 uM range. Predictions far above 16 uM rely on saturation at Vmax.
